scope: Canonical biotech, pharma, and life-sciences terms explicitly discussed across the eight UNLOCK 2026 transcripts: biology, drug discovery and development, clinical science, and laboratory and experimentation vocabulary, plus the life-sciences-leaning entries from scientific data and computing. Split on 2026-08-27 from the combined glossary.json (schemaVersion 1, 271 terms) into this file and glossary.ai-tech.json; term entries are unchanged. Company and person names remain in the conference graph (graph/biotech/). AI/ML method terms, named models, and benchmarks live in glossary.ai-tech.json even when their subject matter is biological.

terms.definition: The absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity properties used to assess whether a molecule could become a safe and effective drug.
aliases: absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity

terms.definition: A molecular building block whose sequence forms a protein.
An immune protein that binds a specific molecular target and can be engineered as a therapeutic.
A therapeutic that links a target-specific antibody to a drug payload so the payload can be delivered to selected cells.
An experimental procedure that measures a biological or chemical property.
A laboratory in which software and robotics can plan, execute, analyze, and iterate experiments with limited human intervention.
Systematic variation caused by differences in experimental runs, sites, protocols, or processing rather than the biology being studied.
The strength of the interaction between two molecules, such as a drug or antibody and its target.
The computational analysis and interpretation of biological data.
A therapeutic produced from or composed of biological material, such as an antibody or recombinant protein.
A measurable biological characteristic used to indicate a state, process, disease, or response to treatment.
A group of diseases characterized by uncontrolled cell growth and the potential to invade or spread to other tissues.
Data produced by controlled interventions that help reveal how changing one factor affects another.
Methods for estimating cause-and-effect relationships rather than simple correlations.
The fundamental structural and functional unit of living organisms.
A population of cells maintained in culture for repeated experimental use.
The molecular and functional condition of a cell at a particular time.
Treatment in which living cells are administered, replaced, or modified to produce a therapeutic effect.
The cell type, tissue, disease state, environment, and experimental conditions in which a cellular response occurs.
Chemical compounds considered as starting points, leads, or candidates in a drug-discovery program.
The stage of medicine development in which a candidate is tested in humans and evidence is assembled for regulatory review.
A predefined patient outcome or measurement used to evaluate a clinical trial.
A measurable change in a patient's disease or health after treatment.
Early evidence in patient data that a treatment may have a meaningful biological or therapeutic effect.
A prospective study in human participants that evaluates a medical intervention.
A public database that aggregates evidence about relationships between human genetic variants and health.
A cycle in which experimental results update a model, which then proposes the next experiments.
A remotely accessible automated laboratory in which users submit experimental workflows through software.
The use of algorithms, models, and computation to study biological systems.
A hypothetical outcome describing what would happen if an intervention or condition were different.
A molecule designed to form a stable covalent bond with its biological target.
The deliberate production of new measurements through experiments, assays, simulations, or observation.
The Cancer Dependency Map, a large resource connecting genetic and molecular features of cancer models to vulnerabilities.
The combined properties that determine whether a candidate can be manufactured, formulated, delivered, tolerated, and advanced as a medicine.
Meaningful biological or clinical variation among patients or samples assigned the same disease label.
An experimental or computational system used to reproduce selected features of a human disease.
The iterative design-make-test-analyze cycle used to improve candidate molecules.
Deoxyribonucleic acid, the molecule that stores hereditary information in most organisms.
The determination of the order of nucleotide bases in DNA.
The relationship between the amount of an intervention and the magnitude of the resulting biological effect.
The process of identifying and optimizing potential therapeutic interventions.
A biological molecule or process whose modulation is expected to produce a therapeutic effect.
Computational, mathematical, or data-analysis work performed without direct physical experimentation.
The degree to which an intervention produces its intended beneficial effect under specified conditions.
Epidermal growth factor receptor, a signaling protein frequently altered and therapeutically targeted in cancer.
The alteration of gene-regulatory marks and programs without changing the underlying DNA sequence.
The genome-wide study of chemical and structural features that regulate gene activity without changing DNA sequence.
Cellular signaling driven by estrogen receptors, important in normal physiology and several cancers.
Experiments performed on living cells, tissues, or organs removed from an organism while preserving aspects of their native organization.
A pattern introduced by measurement or protocol conditions rather than the biological phenomenon of interest.
Contextual information about how, where, when, and under what conditions an experiment was performed.
The United States Food and Drug Administration, which regulates drugs, biologics, medical devices, and related products.
A DNA sequence that contributes to a functional product or regulated biological process.
The deliberate alteration of DNA at selected genomic locations.
The process and measurable level by which information in a gene is used to produce RNA or protein.
The network of relationships and control mechanisms that determines when and how genes are expressed.
The study of genes, heredity, and variation.
The complete genetic material of an organism or cell.
A systematic experiment that alters genes across most or all of the genome to measure their effects.
The large-scale study of genomes, their organization, variation, and function.
Hematoxylin-and-eosin staining, a standard pathology method for visualizing tissue structure.
Data in which each observation contains many measured variables or features.
Automated testing of large numbers of compounds, perturbations, or biological conditions.
The diagnosis and study of disease through microscopic examination of tissue.
The stage in which initial active compounds are confirmed and improved into credible lead series.
The study and use of inherited and acquired genetic variation in people.
A cell that participates in innate or adaptive immune defense.
A regulatory pathway that restrains immune activation and can be therapeutically blocked in cancer.
The cells, tissues, molecules, and processes that protect the body from threats and abnormal cells.
The study of the immune system.
Treatment that activates, redirects, or suppresses immune function to address disease.
Performed computationally, such as a simulation or virtual screen.
Performed outside a living organism in a controlled laboratory system.
Performed within a living organism.
A disease, condition, or patient use for which a therapy is being developed or prescribed.
A molecule that reduces the activity of a biological target or process.
Measurements collected after deliberately changing a variable or applying a perturbation.
A signaling protein and oncogene frequently mutated in cancer and targeted by several drug-discovery programs.
The use of instruments, robotics, and software to execute laboratory workflows with reduced manual handling.
A high-molecular-weight therapeutic such as an antibody, protein, or other biologic.
Iterative improvement of a lead molecule's potency, selectivity, safety, exposure, and developability.
A modeling setting where examples are scarce relative to the complexity of the prediction task.
The biological process through which a treatment produces its effect.
Study focused on the causal molecular and cellular processes that produce a biological outcome.
A non-human species studied experimentally to understand biology that may generalize to other organisms.
A class of therapeutic molecule or intervention, such as a small molecule, antibody, RNA medicine, or cell therapy.
Computational estimation of a molecule's chemical, physical, biological, or safety properties.
The computational or experimental creation and optimization of molecular structures for desired properties.
The observable form, shape, and structural features of cells, tissues, or organisms.
Simultaneous improvement of several candidate properties, such as potency, selectivity, safety, and exposure.
Imaging that measures many protein markers in the same tissue sample while preserving spatial location.
An engineered therapy capable of binding or modulating more than one target or epitope.
An experiment or trial focused on a single individual, often to evaluate a personalized intervention.
The study of the nervous system.
A primate species other than humans used in biological and preclinical research.
A molecular building block of DNA or RNA.
Measurements collected without deliberately assigning an intervention.
Large-scale measurement of a class of biological molecules or features, such as genomes, transcripts, proteins, or epigenetic marks.
The study and treatment of cancer.
A three-dimensional cell culture that reproduces selected structures and functions of an organ or tissue.
A therapy developed for a rare disease or condition.
The capacity of a genetic variant, organism, or biological factor to cause disease.
The study and diagnosis of disease through changes in tissues, cells, and bodily materials.
The division of patients into biologically or clinically meaningful groups, often to predict treatment response.
Measurements obtained directly from patient samples, records, or outcomes.
A pooled screening method that combines genetic perturbations with single-cell RNA sequencing to measure their effects.
A deliberate change to a biological system, such as a gene edit, drug treatment, or environmental alteration.
A collection of measurements describing how biological systems respond to controlled interventions.
The study of how drugs interact with biological systems.
An observable molecular, cellular, organismal, or clinical characteristic.
A commercial arrangement that grants access to a discovery technology, model, dataset, or integrated platform.
Prevention or treatment tailored to molecular, environmental, or clinical differences among patients.
An experimental system used to study disease or treatment effects before human clinical trials.
A folded chain of amino acids that performs structural, catalytic, signaling, or regulatory functions.
Therapeutic removal of a target protein by directing it to a cell's degradation machinery.
The creation or optimization of amino-acid sequences to produce desired protein structures and functions.
The production or measured abundance of a protein in a cell or tissue.
The three-dimensional organization of a protein that helps determine its function and interactions.
A physical or functional association between two proteins.
The large-scale study of proteins, including their abundance, structure, interactions, and modifications.
An aggregate gene-expression profile created by combining measurements from many single cells.
A targeted molecule linked to a radioactive isotope for imaging or therapy.
A disease affecting a small fraction of the population, often with a strong genetic component.
The evidence, methods, and standards used to evaluate the quality, safety, and effectiveness of regulated medical products.
Ribonucleic acid, a family of molecules central to gene expression, regulation, and protein synthesis.
A therapeutic whose active component or mechanism uses RNA.
A sequencing method used to measure RNA molecules and gene-expression patterns.
A laboratory where robotic equipment performs physical experimental operations.
The assessment and management of harmful or unacceptable effects from an intervention.
The degree to which a molecule acts on its intended target more strongly than on other targets.
Determining the ordered bases in DNA or RNA, or by extension the ordered units in another biological polymer.
Measurements resolved to individual cells rather than averaged across a mixed population.
RNA sequencing performed at individual-cell resolution.
A relatively low-molecular-weight organic compound that can modulate a biological target.
The study of biological molecules, cells, and interactions while preserving their location in tissue.
Measurement of gene expression while retaining the spatial position of cells or regions in tissue.
The chemical or biological production of a molecule.
The design and engineering of biological systems or components with new or modified functions.
The study of interacting biological components as integrated systems rather than isolated parts.
A lymphocyte central to adaptive immunity, including helper and cytotoxic immune functions.
The identification of biological processes or molecules that could be therapeutically modulated.
Selection of a specific biological target connected to a disease mechanism.
Ranking potential drug targets by evidence, tractability, safety, and likely therapeutic value.
Experimental confirmation that changing a target produces a relevant and reproducible disease effect.
The interaction between a biological target and a molecule that binds it.
A modality that recruits cellular machinery to selectively eliminate a disease-related protein.
A biotechnology approach or company model built around deep integration of software, data, automation, and biology.
An intervention intended to prevent, treat, or manage disease.
A measure of the separation between doses that produce benefit and doses that produce toxicity.
An organized group of cells and extracellular material that performs related functions.
The capacity of a substance or intervention to cause harmful biological effects.
The complete set of RNA transcripts present in a cell, tissue, or organism under specified conditions.
The large-scale study of RNA transcripts and gene-expression patterns.
Work that connects laboratory discoveries to practical diagnosis, prevention, or treatment in patients.
An abnormal mass of tissue produced by excessive or unregulated cell growth.
The tumor cells, immune cells, stroma, signaling molecules, and physical context surrounding a tumor.
Independent testing that checks whether a result, model, target, or assay is reliable and fit for its intended use.
A single variable antibody domain derived from heavy-chain-only antibodies and used as a compact binding scaffold.
Computational evaluation of many candidate molecules or interventions before physical testing.
Physical experimentation with biological or chemical materials.
Generation of candidate molecules for a previously unseen target without target-specific training or iterative optimization.
